canberra.title: Man sentenced over ‘melee’ outside Higgins unit
canberra.snippet: A chain of “threatening remarks” that started on Christmas Day led to a “melee” outside a Canberra unit, a court ...
canberra.content:
The court heard the 38-year-old and his ex-partner were both injured in the attack. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A chain of “threatening remarks” that started on Christmas Day led to a “melee” outside a Canberra unit, a court has heard.

A 38-year-old man, whom Region has chosen not to name to avoid identifying the victims, faced the ACT Supreme Court for sentencing on Wednesday (22 July).

The man and his former partner began messaging each other on 25 December 2024, before sending each other further messages on 29 December.

“Some of the messages contained acts of violence and those threats passed both ways,” Justice Andrew Muller said.

Later that evening, the ex-partner and four other people drove to the offender’s home in Higgins.

The man went outside his unit to meet the group, before he picked up a 20 centimetre-long knife from the ground.

One of the group hit the man in the head using a metal bar, while his ex-partner struck him with a baseball bat.

The man stabbed her in her left shoulder and used the baseball bat to hit her in the torso.

During sentencing, Justice Muller described this as a marked escalation in the situation, but said it was an attempt at self-defence.

“The use of a knife elevates the seriousness of the offending in that it was a highly dangerous weapon utilised deliberately to cause serious physical harm,” he said.

“I am mindful it was used in circumstances where [the man] had already been struck with blunt force weapons … His use of the knife is thus in the nature of excessive force directed at least in part to defending himself.”

He also described this case as “relatively unique” due to that “self-defence context”.

It was at that point that the male victim went to the car to get a jack handle, but the female victim yelled at him to go back to the car.

“Thereafter, [the offender] approached the vehicle with [the male victim] seated in it. He punched the window adjacent to the driver’s seat whilst yelling at [the other man].”

He then threw a baseball bat at the car.

“Although there were further threatening remarks, the melee essentially ended at that point,” Justice Muller said.

The man pleaded guilty to charges of recklessly inflicting grievous bodily harm (family violence) and common assault in March 2026.

Following the incident, both the offender and his ex-partner were taken to hospital to be treated for their injuries.

The court heard that she spent at least two days in hospital and needed a chest drain to help repair a collapsed lung, while the man had several haematomas and bruising.

Justice Muller said the man was on bail for about five months under “strict” bail conditions.

While he had breached court orders in the past, he noted no breaches were recorded during that period.

The man has spent 319 days in custody before sentencing.

Justice Muller said the man had a traumatic childhood, where he was exposed to alcohol and violence as a child.

He said the man began drinking when he was 13 years old and has been “in and out” of residential programs.

Before his arrest, he was also regularly using cannabis, methamphetamines and MDMA.

The family moved to the NSW South Coast when the man was five, before he returned to the ACT for work when he was 17.

Justice Muller also noted a character reference from his mother, where she described her son as a “kind, caring and compassionate” individual.

In another reference, one of the man’s siblings also described him as caring.

“She observes [that the man] is a devoted father to his children and she believes he is committed to making better choices for himself and his family,” he said.

He was satisfied that the offender has shown remorse for his offending and its impacts on others and said the man acknowledged the damage to the relationship with his ex-partner.

“He has shown some insight into the negative consequences of his resort to violence in this case and the damage it has done to family relations which, although fractured by a separation, were relatively amicable.”

He also said the man’s sentence will be discounted by about 20 per cent in light of his guilty plea.

Justice Muller ultimately handed the man a sentence of imprisonment of two-and-a-half years, with a non-parole period lasting until January 2027.

A charge of possessing an offensive weapon with intent was also taken into account on sentencing, while a transfer charge was withdrawn.

canberra.title: Attorney-General accused of giving herself power to ‘captain’s pick’ judicial officials
canberra.snippet: Tara Cheyne has shot back at allegations she deliberately changed the rules to give herself power to make “captain’s picks&#8...
canberra.content:
The subordinate law changes do include the ability to veto Attorney-General Tara Cheyne’s (pictured) recommended replacements for judicial positions. Photo: ACT Government.

Tara Cheyne has shot back at allegations she deliberately changed the rules to give herself power to make “captain’s picks” for Canberra’s court.

During budget estimates hearings, the Attorney-General was challenged over the direct appointments of Louise Taylor as Chief Magistrate, and Andrew Muller as a resident judge in the Supreme Court.

Shadow Attorney-General Chiaka Barry accused Ms Cheyne of creating a second pathway to appointing judicial figures as a way to give herself power.

“You’ve changed a determination that’s never been done in this way before,” Ms Barry said.

“Do you not see this as a problem, that we risk politicising judicial appointments? You’ve essentially given yourself a power that you’ve never had before.”

The judicial appointment processes were set out in the Magistrates Court (Magistrates Appointment Requirements) Determination 2009 and Supreme Court (Resident Judges Appointment Requirements) Determination 2015 (No 1).

These notifiable instruments were repealed on 26 March, two weeks before two of the judicial officials were announced.

The in-force instruments are now the Magistrates Court (Magistrates Appointment Requirements) Determination 2026 (No 1) and Supreme Court (Resident Judges Appointment Requirements) Determination 2026 (No 1).

Previously judicial appointments could only be made through an expression of interest process but these changes introduced the option for the Attorney-General to directly recommend a person for the job.

Once recommended, a group of stakeholders also has to agreed with the selection. The final determination is then taken to Cabinet.

Ms Cheyne said because of circumstances surrounding the court vacancies, and the candidates put forward, she felt it was more prudent to bypass what could have been a lengthier EOI process.

“We had identified exceptional candidates who met the requisite legal standing, and who had the express support of the profession,” she said.

“It was obvious that if any EOI or panel process was undertaken, that these candidates would be the outcome.

“This made the most sense in these circumstances.”

Ms Cheyne said when she reviewed the notifiable instruments, and considered other advice, she felt the subordinate legislation “needed a refresh anyway”.

“Providing this flexible option, particularly in all of the circumstances as they presented themselves, was eminently sensible in the circumstances,” she said.

“I needed flexibility in unusual circumstances.”

Ms Cheyne rejected the assertion she had made a “captain’s pick”, stating she wouldn’t have done so without knowing she had “express support” of the candidates from justice stakeholders.

There is a veto option within the Attorney-General’s new powers.

The proposed appointee can only be put forward for final determination if they have the endorsement of the ACT Bar Association, the ACT Law Society, and either the Chief Magistrate (for the appointment of a magistrate) or Chief Justice (for the appointment of the Chief Magistrate).

Ms Cheyne said this meant she didn’t have complete power in the process.

“[The selection] doesn’t go anywhere if just one of those [listed above] says, ‘no, I have concerns about that person’,” she said.

“Only if they all confirm support [does] that recommendation proceed to Cabinet.”

Responsible ministers are allowed to make determinations to amend, repeal or replace insubordinate legislation (or instruments).

Ms Cheyne had sought advice from the Solicitor General before making the changes.

Ms Barry said that wasn’t the issue.

“I get you have the power to [make the change] … the fact that you [can] doesn’t mean you should do it,” she said.

“[This has] never been done in the history of the Territory … in a time where we have a decline in the trust of our institutions, it is incumbent on us that we all protect the integrity of our institutions, and particularly on me to ask these questions, so I am doing my job.”

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton called the moves by Ms Cheyne a “fundamental breach of convention”.

“For the first time, the Attorney-General can hand-pick judges without open competition,” he said.

“We call on the Attorney-General to immediately restore a single, open and merit-based appointment process.”

The disputed vacancies were created when Chief Magistrate Lorraine Walker and Justice Chrissa Loukas-Karlsson announced their retirements.

Ms Taylor was the acting Chief Magistrate before her permanent appointment, and Mr Muller had been an Acting Justice since April 2025.

Ms Taylor’s move from the Supreme Court left another vacancy. An EOI process for this position was opened on 10 April and former ACT Director of Public Prosecutions Jon White was announced as a new Supreme Court resident judge on 19 June.

canberra.title: Napoleon’s botanical army continues its Aussie invasion
canberra.snippet: The European willow is one of South Eastern Australia’s most invasive environmental weeds and, according to legend, its arrival in ...
canberra.content:
Willows are a blight on Australia’s waterways but represent a curious connection to European history. Photo: Wagga Wagga City Council.

The European willow is one of South Eastern Australia’s most invasive environmental weeds and, according to legend, its arrival in the colony of NSW in the 19th century is linked to Europe’s most successful general.

Where Napoleon Bonaparte famously stormed the ancient capitals of Europe, his willows took root in the colonies as a quiet tribute to the late Emperor before steadily conquering our regional waterways.

New research into these living memorials has added a fresh Aussie twist to the Emperor’s final days, and suggests things could have turned out very differently.

An article in the Wagga Wagga Advertiser in August 1903 lays out some of the local mythology.

“We regret to learn that the original willow tree at Kenmore Homestead near Goulburn is succumbing to old age,” it begins.

“This tree was planted by Mr Balcombe, who was custodian of Napoleon at St Helena, and was grown from a cutting taken by him from Napoleon’s grave.

“The historic old tree was the stock from which all the willows on the Wollondilly, Murray and Murrumbidgee rivers and their tributaries were propagated.”

William Balcombe was a colonial administrator with the East India Company and served as the first treasurer of the colony of New South Wales.

Before migrating to Australia, he had served on the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena where Napoleon Bonaparte spent the final years of his life in exile after his defeat at Waterloo.

The family hosted the former ‘Emperor of the French’ in their home for several months, where the general famously befriended their daughter Betsy.

When Napoleon died in 1821, he was buried beside a spring beneath a grove of weeping willows. The legend goes that this was his favourite spot on the island and he was particularly fond of these trees.

In the years after his death, the island became something of a tourism hotspot with visitors from around the world eagerly collecting cuttings from the graveside as living souvenirs of the visit.

Large populations of willows in parts of South Africa, New Zealand, and Australia are said to originate from Napoleon’s tomb.

Napoleon’s tomb on the island of St Helena by Augustus Earle. Photo: NLA Collection.

Researchers Ekaterina Heath and Emma Gleadhill have been taking a closer look at the stories surrounding these historic trees and in their paper, Roots of the myth: Napoleon’s willows, memory and empire, they have highlighted another Australian connection that brings the legend full circle.

Shortly after Napoleon’s death, medical officer Dr Thomas Shortt wrote that he had “desired to be buried in Europe, but should his request be denied, he had fixed on a spot that is now preparing to receive his earthly remains, under some Botany Bay willows”.

Several sources agree that Napoleon’s favourite tree had been a Botany Bay willow, better known as the Australian wattle!

His former wife Josephine was known to collect Australian flora and fauna and among the wattles and gum trees at the Chateau de Malmaison outside Paris, she kept a kangaroo and even managed to successfully breed black swans.

Heath and Gleadhill point to the writings of another doctor, Francois Antommarchi, to explain why Napoleon’s dying wish was altered in the wake of a huge storm.

“The willow under which Napoleon usually sat to enjoy the fresh air had yielded to the tempest; our plantations were torn up by the roots, and lay scattered about,” Antommarchi wrote.

“A single gum-tree still resisted, when a whirlwind seized it, tore it up, and laid it prostrate in the mud. It seemed as if none of the things the Emperor had valued were to survive him.”

So instead, Napoleon was laid under the weeping willows that are also a traditional European symbol of mourning and lament for a fallen hero.

How different things could have been if the yellow-flowered Australian acacia had become the source of the thousands of living souvenirs that were transported across the world!

In 1932, the original graveside trees on St Helena were in such bad shape that cuttings from along the Wollondilly River in NSW, that had originated from William Balcombe’s tree at Goulburn, were sent back to repopulate the grove.

In one final ecological twist of fate, in the same way that the European willow has left a destructive legacy on the Australian landscape, the Botany Bay wattle is now a notorious environmental weed on St Helena.

Touché!

Original Article published by Chris Roe on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Turn ‘safe phones’ off before AusAlert test, cautions Minister
canberra.snippet: People who have secret or concealed “safe phones” should turn them off before the upcoming AusAlert warning system test if they want them...
canberra.content:
The AusAlert emergency warning system will be test broadcast to all mobile phones on Monday. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

People who have secret or concealed “safe phones” should turn them off before the upcoming AusAlert warning system test if they want them to remain undetected.

The new emergency warning system will be tested nationally on Monday (27 July) at 2 pm AEST, now that nine community-based trials across the country have been declared “successful” and have provided “valuable insights”.

Following the Australia-wide test, the system will then officially go live in October.

The alert works by broadcasting a 10-second siren to mobile phones, along with a ‘systems alert’ rather than a text message, in areas affected by an emergency.

But Monday’s test is going to everyone with a mobile phone.

Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain described AusAlert on Wednesday (22 July) as a “milestone” that will deliver emergency alerts to more people in a “more timely manner” than the existing text-based emergency alert system.

But she cautioned that it will make a loud sound on people’s mobile phones, so anyone wanting to keep their devices secret should turn them off or switch them to aeroplane mode one hour before the test.

They should then keep their mobiles switched off or on flight mode until 24 hours after the test, the minister said.

The alert will sound through phones that are simply on silent, or a do not disturb mode.

“The national test will assess system-wide performance, checking the system can broadcast at scale to compatible devices in near real time without network congestion,” she said.

“The national test also provides an opportunity for Australians to familiarise themselves with AusAlert before alerts are sent during local or national disasters, including natural hazards such as bushfires, floods or cyclones or other security threats.

“The system was developed in response to the 2020 royal commission into national natural disaster arrangements, which identified the need for a more modern, reliable, and nationally consistent public warning capability.

“Cell broadcast technology, which is used successfully in 35 other countries, is that technology, especially during fast-moving and unpredictable emergencies.”

Hidden phones can be part of a safety plan for people at risk of domestic violence.

Wesnet (Women’s Services Network) has echoed the minister’s advice about turning concealed phones off or to flight mode during Monday’s test, but added that once AusAlert is live, bigger decisions will need to be made.

“Once the national emergency alert system is officially in place from October, people using hidden phones, as part of a safety plan, will need to make their own decision about the risks of having their phones on, on a permanent basis or whether it’s safer for them to keep their hidden phones off when they’re not in use,” Wesnet CEO Karen Bentley has stated.

Domestic violence perpetrators often use spyware and tracking apps to monitor the whereabouts and activities of their victims.

Wesnet and some other charities distribute repurposed smartphones to help women and children secretly escape abuse and coordinate safety plans.

Ms McBain met with her state and territory counterparts on Wednesday for the National Emergency Management Ministers’ Meeting.

Following the meeting, the federal minister said Monday’s test will assess the technology’s ability to broadcast warnings at scale, but that AusAlert will run along the existing emergency alert system for the upcoming high-risk weather season to make sure people without mobile phones can still get warnings.

But it will be up to each jurisdiction if they use both systems into the future.

“It’s one of the reasons those two systems will run alongside each other for this high-risk weather season,” Ms McBain said.

“Obviously, it would be great if we could use both systems to make sure that people are getting advice and notification if we need to advise people in those critical alert situations.

“But that will be a decision for emergency service agencies who are in control of whatever that disaster may be at the time.”

The minister downplayed suggestions that both the AusAlert and state-based system being used at the same time could create confusion.

Getting as much information as possible at times of disaster is always welcome.

“If they get that through a text message or an alert and notification on their phone, they are grateful,” she said.

“They get that from their emergency broadcasters; they love that.

“This is another tool in the toolkit, and it’s incredibly important that people continue to listen to the advice of emergency services.”

Ministers from both Queensland and Western Australia raised concerns in the meeting about people with landlines, which are more dominantly used in remote areas, being notified of disasters.

Concerns were also raised in the meeting about messages only being sent in English.

“A siren is pretty effective, and absolutely moves across language barriers,” Ms McBain said.

“People know when they hear a siren that there is an emergency happening.”

canberra.title: St Edmund’s pedestrian crossing officially opens but permanent 40 km/h zone debate weighs on
canberra.snippet: A new pedestrian crossing on Canberra Avenue, where two schoolboys were hit by a stolen vehicle in March 2025, is now operating, but deba...
canberra.content:
A new pedestrian crossing on Canberra Avenue, where two school students were hit by a car in March last year, is now in operation, but debate continues about whether the speed limit should change too. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

A new pedestrian crossing on Canberra Avenue, where two schoolboys were hit by a stolen vehicle in March 2025, is now operating, but debate rages on around what the speed limit for the area should be.

Works on the new signalled crossing began in May and required motorists using the road to slow down to 40 km/h, down from the original 60 km/h drivers must otherwise follow.

The promise for the crossing was made after two schoolboys were seriously injured by a driver high on meth in March last year. However, despite the roadworks reducing the speed limit by 20 km/h, once all the roadworks in the area are completed, the limit will revert to 60 km/h.

St Edmund College’s new principal, James Keeley, who started this week, said the crossing will provide safety for students of the college as well as St Clare’s College, but believes a permanent 40 km/h zone will better ensure student safety.

“We firmly believe that westbound traffic on Canberra Avenue would function well as a school zone during school operating hours,” he said.

“The section of road adjacent to St Clare’s and St Edmund’s is approximately 500 metres long, meaning a reduction from 60 km/h to 40 km/h during school zone times would add around 15 seconds to a driver’s journey.

“In our view, that is a very reasonable trade-off when balanced against the safety of the large number of students, families and staff who use the area each day. Student safety must remain the overriding consideration.

“Student safety is our number one priority, so the new crossing is a great addition, not only for our students but also for students at St Clare’s and the broader community.

“It will make crossing this busy road much safer for everyone. We have already noticed that it provides a clearer and safer route for pedestrians crossing Canberra Avenue, particularly during the busy morning drop-off and afternoon pick-up periods.”

In March 2025, a man high on meth hit two students of St Edmund’s College, leading to the push for a pedestrian crossing. Photo: Supplied.

St Clare’s College Principal Dr Anne Cleary also echoed Mr Keeley’s calls for safety while also highlighting the benefits of the new crossing.

“There are obvious benefits for students who need to cross the road as part of their journey to and from school each day,” she said.

“In the longer run there could also be advantages for parents who perhaps choose to drop students off on the opposite side of the road, helping reduce congestion around the school.”

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said the Canberra Avenue crossing is a good first step to addressing safety issues, but he believes the speed limit in the area should be reduced from 60 km/h to 40 km/h.

“Both school communities have been calling for road safety improvements along Canberra Avenue for decades. It’s great to finally see this crossing in operation,” he said.

“While this wouldn’t have prevented what happened to Aiden and Aaron [the two students injured last year], which is why there’s been a push for an overpass, I know the boys and their families will be pleased to see something positive come from that terrible day last March.

“The government should also listen to community calls for a 40 km/h zone along this stretch.”

Mr Emerson said the ACT Government needs to think of the long-term benefits and work together as a community to ensure kids can walk and ride safely to school.

“We know the wide-ranging social, health and environmental benefits of prioritising active travel, and we have to be willing to realise those benefits around our schools despite the strong temptation to prioritise the convenience of car travel.

“The need for improved road safety measures and active travel connections will only increase in this area as the proposed Hume Circle precinct gets developed.”

australia.title: ALP announces sweeping changes to student work placements as Gaza war looms large at party conference
australia.snippet: Anthony Albanese will cast ‘practical’ policies as the key to countering the anxiety and frustration in Australia Get our breaking news e...
australia.content:
Students in 10 fields including physiotherapy, speech pathology and clinical psychology will receive financial assistance to complete mandatory placements under a major expansion of the federal government’s paid work experience program.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will make the announcement in a speech to open the Labor national conference on Thursday, which will cast “practical” policies as the key to combating the anxiety and frustration gripping the electorate.

Labor MPs, trade unionists and rank-and-file members will use the triennial conference to thrash out the party’s policy agenda for the next three years.

A high-level commitment to increase taxes on gas exports and wind back fuel tax credits are set to be enshrined in the official party platform, which sets a long-term expectation – rather than an immediate requirement – for the parliamentary party to act.

Deals between factional powerbrokers are expected to avert major flare-ups during the three-day conference, although there is tension ahead of Saturday’s debate on the party’s position on Israel and Palestine.

Jewish groups and Israel’s embassy in Canberra are publicly putting pressure on the party to water-down the draft text, which they claim is not critical enough of Hamas’ role in the Gaza war, while pro-Palestine supporters within Labor are pushing to strengthen the language.

Senior Labor figures believe the draft version strikes the right balance and are reluctant to bend to either group, meaning a contested debate on the conference floor is unlikely.

A Students for Palestine protest calling for a stop to arms trade with Israel – which the government disputes occurs – is planned for Thursday afternoon outside the Adelaide Convention Centre, which will have beefed-up security for the 3000-person conference.

In his speech, Albanese will attempt to draw a clear contrast between Labor and its political opponents, in particular One Nation, warning that “raging against a system” without a plan to fix it doesn’t “take the country forward”.

“I understand that for many Australians right now, looking to the future runs second to the immediate pressures they are under,” the prime minister will tell the conference, according to a draft version supplied to Guardian Australia.

“It is a challenge confronting governments and democracies right around the world.

“That is why our focus remains squarely on helping with the cost of living, on the practical measures that matter to people and make a positive difference to their lives.”

The prime minister will announce students in ten extra courses will receive up to $338.60 a week during their clinical or professional placements, starting 1 July 2027.

The courses are: clinical psychology, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech pathology, paramedicine, radiography, pharmacy, rehabilitation therapies, audiology podiatry.

The program is currently limited to teaching, nursing, midwifery and social work.

The expansion comes after pressure from MPs including David Pocock and Helen Haines, who last month tabled a 43,000-person signature calling for allied health courses to be included.

“This is how Labor governs,” Albanese will tell the conference. “We deal with the here and now in a way that builds for the future too. We navigate the rough seas, while always keeping our eyes on the horizon.”

After Kate Ellis is installed as the new Labor president on Thursday morning, the 400 conference delegates will start debating the text of the 126-page draft platform, starting with economic and climate policies on Thursday.

Delegates from the left and right factions held lengthy meetings on Wednesday to discuss their positions on various topics.

The section of the draft platform that commits Labor to securing a “fairer return” for natural resources is expected to feature in the final text, effectively binding the Albanese government to eventually act on the campaign to increase taxes on gas exports.

Left faction sources were on Wednesday night optimistic a proposal to “remove disincentives for decarbonisation” would also make the final text after it was excluded from the draft version.

The grassroots Labor Environment Action Network (LEAN) is pushing the amendment as part of a campaign to cap fuel tax credits for mining companies, which has won the support of hundreds of local branches and Labor MP Jerome Laxale.

Even if the amendments succeed, the government is unlikely to move quickly on fuel tax credits or a gas tax due to the uncertainty the Middle East conflict has caused to the global oil market.

The left is discussing pushing for even stronger positions in tackling online gambling harm, including a national regulator, ahead a scheduled debate on Friday.

The draft platform already goes further than the government’s gambling advertising legislation with a commitment to address inducements offered by wagering companies.

A ban on inducements and the establishment of a national gambling regulator were among several recommendations from the landmark Murphy report that were omitted from the the government’s bill, which is set to be debated when federal parliament returns next month.

australia.title: Australia to warn China it won’t be bullied by ‘provocative‘ actions as it builds military and nuclear arsenal
australia.snippet: Foreign minister Penny Wong will deliver speech criticising China’s recent launch of a nuclear-capable submarine-launched missile Get our...
australia.content:
Penny Wong will warn China that Australia and other neighbouring nations will not be bullied by its “provocative” actions, after its involvement in another “destabilising and dangerous” incident this week.

The foreign affairs minister – who will deliver the address on Thursday in the Philippines, where the 59th Asean foreign minister’s meeting is being held – will also caution world leaders against placing a toll on the strait of Hormuz after both Iran and the US threatened to do amid the protracted conflict.

The speech comes as the crisis in the Middle East escalates once again, driving up fuel prices by 40 cents in three weeks amid dwindling global oil reserves.

Off the back of China’s launch of a nuclear-capable submarine-launched missile in the South China Sea earlier in July, Wong will say the test “came with too little information and notification”.

“It comes in the context of China’s rapid military buildup, including of its nuclear arsenal, without the transparency or reassurance the region expects,” the foreign minister will say.

“Which is why Australia has described the test as provocative and destabilising.”

Wong met with China’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, on the sidelines of Asean on Tuesday night AEST in their 12th meeting.

Wong had earlier criticised China’s conduct as “destabilising and dangerous” after the Philippine military accused the China Coast Guard of clubbing a Filipino sailor with a baton on Monday on a disputed shoal in the South China Sea.

“We will continue to register our concerns about China’s vessels engaging in destabilising and dangerous conduct in the South China Sea, including towards Philippine, Vietnamese, Malaysian, and Indonesian vessels,” Wong will say on Thursday.

China’s long-range missile test in the South Pacific happened just hours after Australia signed a defence agreement with Fiji, inciting widespread condemnation. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, expressed concern at the missile’s long-range capabilities and the possibility to cause “considerable, considerable damage were it to be weaponised”.

In Manila, Wong will also warn the region will suffer if the strait of Hormuz is “weaponised” and the US and Iran fail to maintain a ceasefire.

Heavy strikes have resumed between the warring nations with the US launching consecutive rounds on Iran in an attempt to force the strait’s reopening.

Iran’s president on Tuesday said the country is in a “full-scale war” after the US expanded its aerial campaign and Tehran struck Washington’s Gulf allies. The Iran-allied Houthis in Yemen have also announced a blockade of Saudi ports.

The renewed outbreak of fighting has sent the international Brent crude benchmark surging by 23% over the past two weeks and back within reach of $US90 a barrel.

The surge in cost has pushed diesel above 220 cents per litre and petrol above 187 cents in some Australian cities. Luke Yeaman, the Commonwealth Bank chief economist, has predicted the federal government may have to restore the fuel excise discount back to 32 cents.

Wong will tell the audience much of the region was fuel- and energy-dependent on the strait of Hormuz, presenting a “grave challenge”.

“Across south-east Asia, energy prices have spiked, costs for families and businesses increased, and we continue to see ongoing pressure on food production,” Wong will say.

“The strait of Hormuz shows what we in this region have always understood. That people suffer when a strait is weaponised. And we all know that the costs of tolls on any chokepoint would not be solely economic.

“Our people depend on straits and sea lanes remaining open.”

Wong will tell Asean nations their assistance in plugging Australia’s supply and trade gaps during the conflict is for the region’s benefit.

“Because what goes to Australia as fuel and fertiliser comes back to the region as food,” she will say.

With additional reporting by Patrick Commins

australia.title: Prosecutors in Alan Jones trial will argue he showed a pattern of targeting ‘significantly younger men’
australia.snippet: The veteran broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two of sexual touching allegedly committed against s...
australia.content:
Alan Jones allegedly squeezed the bottom of a young man he had just met at a fashion show which made the complainant feel “very uncomfortable”, the New South Wales local court has heard in pre-trial evidence which can now be reported.

The 85-year-old former broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two of sexual touching between 2003 and 2020. He has said the charges are “all either baseless or they distort the truth”.

On Wednesday, Judge Glenn Walsh lifted a suppression order on the crown case and the tendency and coincidence evidence, which is admissible at the trial beginning on 3 August and expected to run for four months.

Walsh said Jones now faces a total of 22 charges “said to have been committed against six complainants”.

Prosecutors last week argued they should be allowed to show there is a pattern of alleged behaviour by Jones involving the targeting of “significantly younger men” in his professional and social circle.

The prosecution submitted it is “improbable” that two similar accounts of Jones allegedly touching a complainant’s penis while driving would be “untrue”. Each complainant was driving a car and there was “no reciprocity prior to the touching”, the court heard.

The judge accepted that none of the complainants had any prior knowledge of each other.

“No complainant has any relevant association with any other complainant,” Walsh said.

Two of the six complainants told police they were assaulted on the first occasion they met Jones: one at a fashion show and one at a fundraising meeting.

In the second case, the man told police that while he was talking Jones placed his hand on the top of his leg and rested it on his bottom.

Other complainants had a relationship where the defendant was a mentor or benefactor, the court heard.

Two complainants had a relationship with Jones from a young age which evolved from a professional one to a friendship over time.

The defence had applied for a suppression order, submitting their concern that reporting of the allegations and the tendency and coincidence arguments may be read by a complainant and may prejudice the hearing.

In making his decision to lift the suppression order, Walsh said “no material has been presented to show that any media reporting to date has not been fair and accurate”.

Walsh said Jones has the presumption of innocence. “It is the prosecution that bear the onus of proof throughout, beyond reasonable doubt, for each element of each offence as charged,” he said.

The prosecution’s application to call two witnesses who refused to give a statement to police was denied.

The radio host, who denies the charges, was charged in November 2024 after an investigation by the Sydney Morning Herald journalist Kate McClymont.

That’s where we’ll leave today’s live coverage.

Court hands landmark win for low-paid Domino’s workers in underpayment class action

Domino’s Pizza could pay significant compensation after a landmark Federal Court ruling in favour of franchise workers.

The federal court found the pizza giant misled franchisees when it ordered them to underpay thousands of drivers and in-store staff under outdated employment agreements over five years that excluded key entitlements.

The ruling follows a class action brought by former Domino’s delivery driver Riley Gall in 2019, alleging underpayment of wages under the Australian Consumer Law for loss caused by misleading and deceptive conduct. Gall said:

This isn’t just a win for me. It’s always been about justice for the thousands of others who were exploited and not paid the amount that they deserved under the correct award. Many of them will still be in those positions where the money will really help.

Lawyer for the plaintiff Brett Spiegel said the judgment gave Domino’s franchise employees “the justice they deserve”. Spiegel said:

Riley Gall has shown incredible courage and dedication in bringing this case and persevering over more than six years to get to this day.

This landmark victory highlights the harm widespread and systemic wage underpayment inflicts on a vulnerable labour force. It is a timely reminder for employers to pay their workers what they are owed under the applicable award or agreement.”

The class action covers delivery drivers and in-store workers employed by Domino’s Australian franchisees between 2013 and 2018. A further hearing will be held to decide group member claims.

What we learned – Wednesday 22 July

That’s where we’ll leave today’s live coverage.

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, says the state’s Labor party is under threat from One Nation and “we’ve got to fight for those votes”.

  • Barnaby Joyce has appeared on the Today Show this morning to the backing track of “who let the dogs out”, to clear the record on a bizarre tirade against his dog on Monday evening during a 7.30 interview.

  • A 16-year-old boy has been charged with the murder of his mother after he allegedly stabbed her at a home in Perth, Western Australia, and seriously injured his 12-year-old sister who managed to flee to get help.

  • The CEO of Wesnet, the national peak body for specialist women’s domestic and family violence services, provided advice for women and children experiencing domestic and family violence, who may have hidden phones as part of their safety plan ahead of the AusAlert warning system test this coming Monday at 2pm AEST.

  • Pauline Hanson has copped backlash from politicians for controversial comments made on domestic violence this morning.

  • Millions of Australians may have had data accessed by hackers after Origin Energy confirmed it is investigating a cybersecurity incident.

  • Victoria police assistant commissioner Christopher Gilbert told the antisemitism royal commission that police have seen an increase in antisemitic incidents since the Hamas terror attack of 7 October 2023.

Thanks for joining us, see you tomorrow morning!

Andrew Messenger

Queensland’s domestic violence minister responds to calls to step down over buried report

Queensland’s domestic violence minister Amanda Camm has responded to calls for her to step down amid mounting pressure over revelations the government buried a report by victim-survivors of domestic violence.

Camm commissioned the report, which was heavily critical of police responses and called for a “civilian review mechanism” to escalate complaints about police.

A summary report “developed for broader distribution” was prepared and the working group finished in December. The Guardian has seen the report – you can read our reporting here – and the Labor opposition has called for Camm to be sacked.

Camm responded with a written statement on Wednesday, saying:

The summary report was developed from the final report to protect the identity and safety of working group members.

The intent of the working group was to advise the new government, following the election, and identify and highlight gaps in the system.

The report was released exactly as was promised and intended [sic] to external agencies in May, so they could begin work on delivering reforms to ensure more women are safer sooner.

While Labor had spent a decade failing to deliver real outcomes for domestic violence victims, the intention of the working group was provide victims with a voice directly to a government who for the first time had a focus on delivering genuine outcomes.

  • In Australia, domestic and family violence counselling is available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org

Ima Caldwell

Police database has limitations tracking antisemitic incidents, royal commission told

The inquiry turned to how Victoria police tracks hate crimes, examining whether the force’s primary database (LEAP) adequately flags the specific character of antisemitic or Islamophobic offences.

Assistant commissioner Christopher Gilbert acknowledged that while narrative detail is captured in the system, rapid data extraction remains limited on existing infrastructure.

When asked directly if he believed there was room for improvement in police data collection, Gilbert said:

Yes, I do.

However, he said police do not rely solely on database metrics to assess risk to the public:

I think we’re in a very strong position now …

My view is that we have multiple sources of information relevant to risks to community … Always better data would be an advantage, but I think we have in our possession – in addition to the data that we do have – other material which would actually help us, and it does to this day, to assess risk.

Gilbert highlighted “on the ground relationships” with local synagogues, schools and peak bodies as vital. He said the Community Security Group (CSG) Victoria is a “core community stakeholder” with whom police maintain strong engagement.

Following this public testimony, counsel assisting applied to close the session to discuss confidential details regarding information-sharing protocols between Victoria police and CSG Victoria.

That’s where we’ll leave today’s coverage of the antisemitism royal commission today. We’ll be here to cover tomorrow’s witness testimony.

Donna Lu

Woodside’s North West Shelf extension challenged in federal court

Friends of Australian Rock Art today opened their case challenging the approval of Woodside’s North West Shelf extension in the federal court.

The Australian Conservation Foundation and Fara are this week running concurrent court challenges against the extension’s approval by the federal environment minister, Murray Watt. According to ACF, the project would see about 4bn tonnes of CO2 released into the atmosphere – equivalent to about 10 years of Australia’s annual emissions.

Fara is arguing Watt did not properly identify the risks of the project to the Murujuga Indigenous rock art complex – a landscape of more than a million petroglyphs dating back 50,000 years, including the oldest known image of a human face.

It is also arguing that Watt made errors in the way he considered the economic benefits of the project.

Fara’s legal counsel, Sashi Maharaj KC, told the court that the economic considerations provided by the minister in his statement of reasons for the approval were “shambolic”, and that “the whole statement of reasons is highly unsatisfactory such that the decision is impeachable”.

She said:

This is a clear case where both economic benefits and economic detriments must be considered.

You can’t cherry pick benefits … the balancing exercise is skewed by cherry picking the benefits in the manner the minister has.

The hearing continues.

Victoria police report rise in antisemitic incidents since 7 October 2023

Ima Caldwell

Victoria police assistant commissioner Christopher Gilbert told the antisemitism royal commission that police have seen an increase in antisemitic incidents since the Hamas terror attack of 7 October 2023.

Asked if there had been a rise in incidents, Gilbert said his “anecdotal observation is yes” and that “there are some data sources that may indicate that’s the case as well”.

Gilbert has led Victoria’s Southern Metro region since December 2023, covering 10 local government areas and roughly a quarter of the state’s population. He told the inquiry that Operation Park – the overarching operational framework for Jewish and Muslim community safety across Victoria – was central to police resourcing.

I would characterise the changes over the last two-and-a-half years as having seen Victoria police deploy far more resources far more often relevant to the safety of the Jewish community.

Gilbert said resourcing has remained high and consistent following major security events.

We were deploying, I think, reasonably against our assessment of threat, but we’ve certainly escalated those deployments … which sees us now deploying [more] than we ever have before.

Since October 2023, police have logged almost 18,000 discrete tasks relevant to community sites of interest – with almost 15,000 of those located in Melbourne’s inner south.

Josh Burns joins condemnation of Hanson’s domestic violence comments

Labor MP Josh Burns has accused Pauline Hanson of “speaking before thinking” after her controversial comments on domestic violence.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Burns said it was “not good enough” that Hanson was “victim-blaming”.

It is a serious matter that too many Australian women face a wicked choice between remaining in a home that is unsafe, or facing financial destitution, financial uncertainty and homelessness.

For someone who is parading themselves as a leader of this country, I think our country is better than victim-blaming and trying to somehow put this on the victims.

Cait Kelly

Privatised job providers failing unemployed Australians, according to new report

A new report into Australia’s employment services sector has revealed that privatised job providers are being used to enrich owners, while failing the very people they are meant to help: unemployed Australians.

An investigation by the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research (CICTAR) into employment services, which receive $5.5bn in public money each year, has revealed huge companies in the sector lack transparency and use aggressive tax minimisation, large dividend payouts, offshore-related party payments, tax havens, and opaque financial reporting to extract profits from the system.

The report said:

It’s no secret that Australia’s system of privatised employment services has failed.

The Howard-era system fills the pockets of private equity and millionaires, while leaving jobseekers without work.

In May, the federal employment minister, Amanda Rishworth, announced changes to the system, but said for-profit service providers would remain a part of it.

Antipoverty Centre spokesperson Jay Coonan said:

This industry has been draining public coffers for decades now with little scrutiny thanks to their deep connections to political parties and powerful people – that is well documented in the media and on their websites.

This is the government’s largest procurement outside of the defence portfolio, with $5bn a year going to companies who are subject to little oversight while they use welfare penalties to extract profit from poor people.

Duniam backs tougher laws to block return of suspected Islamic State fighter

Jonno Duniam has echoed opposition leader Angus Taylor’s calls for the federal government to issue temporary exclusion orders to prevent an Australian member of Islamic State from returning home.

It comes after The Australian reported that Australian medical doctor Tareq Kamleh, known as “Dr Jihad”, who was presumed dead, is one of 13 Australian men imprisoned in an Iraqi jail and hoping to return home.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, the shadow home affairs minister dismissed the government’s claims that it is “constrained by the powers and limitations of the temporary exclusion orders regime”.

Well, the one option they do have is to revisit the laws we currently have.

“If we need to strengthen the laws to keep someone who, frankly, [made the] decision this individual did to travel to Syria, to support Islamic State, to be a propaganda mouthpiece for them, to, frankly, practice evil in the way he has, I really don’t want him back here. So, I say to the government that if you need to strengthen the laws, bring us into the tent, we will work with you on whatever it takes to strengthen our laws, to keep someone as insidious as that out of our country.

Duniam condemns Hanson’s domestic violence comments

Shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, has condemned Pauline Hanson’s comments on domestic violence, calling the interview “rather garbled”.

Appearing on radio in Brisbane this morning, the One Nation leader was asked about men who abuse their partners. She said it was “wrong, but it’s also a two-way street”.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Duniam said:

I think we have to be very careful about how we speak when you’re a community leader, when you’re a lawmaker. You need to demonstrate empathy. You need to understand people’s experiences. And I understand the point she’s making about how different people will be affected in different ways, but her conveying of the message she conveyed was very poor and can have a detrimental impact, in my view.

Asked whether he believed women were more often the victims of domestic violence, he said:

Yes, sure, the stats are there, you can’t argue with those statistics. To try and pretend that it is a case otherwise is a fool’s errand, and doesn’t help deal with the situation.

All homeless people in Wilks Park camp have been offered accommodation, NSW minister says

Following up on earlier reporting on council rangers in the regional town of Wagga threatening homeless residents with $1,100 eviction notices.

NSW housing and homelessness minister, Rose Jackson said:

Everyone deserves to be treated with dignity and respect regardless of their housing situation.

Our immediate priority is making sure everyone has access to safe accommodation and the support they need.

Every homeless person camped in Wilks Park and Wagga Wagga Beach have been offered accommodation. Not everyone accepts our offers of support, but Homes NSW staff will keep trying.

I’ve always said that hotels and motels should be a last resort. Purpose-built crisis accommodation is always preferable, because it comes with those wraparound supports that help people get back on the path to stable housing.

That’s why we created the $100 million Homelessness Innovation Fund and why we are investing $130 million to build more crisis beds in NSW.

Undoing a decade of neglect in housing and homelessness won’t happen overnight, but we are doing the work, backed by record investment in both housing and homelessness.

Rebel Wilson wins defamation case brought by co-star after bitter dispute

After a blistering dispute that spanned continents and years, Hollywood A-lister Rebel Wilson has been found not to have defamed her co-star in a series of social media posts, AAP reports.

The Pitch Perfect star was sued by Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut film The Deb.

After the verdict on Wednesday, Wilson thanked the judge and the Australian legal system, saying the process had tested her and reinforced her belief in “standing up for what I believe is right, while continuing to create work that brings people joy”.

Read more here:

Ima Caldwell

VicPol counter-terrorism chief questioned on synagogue security and data gaps

Acting Cmdr Kelvin Gale, head of Victoria police’s counter-terrorism group (CTG), has outlined gaps in hate crime data collection and event classification during testimony at the antisemitism royal commission.

Questioned by counsel assisting Richard Lancaster SC, Gale said CTG does not routinely classify synagogues as “crowded places” under national security guidelines, noting external precincts can fit the definition as people gather and move through them.

He said a “state-led” event status, for example, the visit of Israeli president Isaac Herzog, is determined by statewide resourcing demands rather than threat levels alone. “It’s not about the risk or the importance,” Gale testified. “It’s about the resourcing commitment.”

There is no automated data tracker for antisemitic or Islamophobic incidents, though Gale noted the Law Enforcement Assistance Program (LEAP) database has a “prejudice-motivated crime” tag officers can use at their discretion. He said accurate data could give police greater confidence when making resourcing decisions.

Gale added that CTG manages the Victoria Police Shield Network, distributing intelligence updates to about 1,000 security managers, including the Community Security Group (CSG), though he could not recall whether CSG representatives attend CTG’s bi-annual Crowded Places Network Forums. Over the past 12 months, CTG has conducted six active armed defender exercises at major public venues, including GMHBA Stadium and Broadmeadow Shopping Centre.

Christopher Knaus

Greens join calls for greater whistleblower protection

The Greens justice spokesperson, David Shoebridge, has joined calls for greater protection for witnesses involved in royal commissions after revelations that a key robodebt whistleblower was suing her department over alleged threats.

Jeannie-Marie Blake, a Services Australia employee who repeatedly raised concerns about the robodebt scheme, is suing her department for alleged threats she received from superiors before and after explosive evidence to the robodebt royal commission in 2023.

Her lawyers at the Human Rights Law Centre, which runs a dedicated whistleblower support service, say the case raises broader concerns about gaps in protection for public servants giving evidence to royal commissions. A 2022 government review of the royal commissions act previously found it lacked any power to impose a civil penalty on a person who causes detriment to a witness giving evidence to a royal commission.

Shoebridge said Blake’s case showed the need for greater whistleblower protection. He said:

For over four years now the Greens have been pushing for comprehensive whistleblower protections that apply wherever, and whenever, the truth is told in good faith.

This latest example shows why these laws are more needed than ever. It also shows why we need to stop pretending Labor will be better, and instead build an alternative power base in parliament to replace them.

The office of the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said current laws governing royal commissions already contained strong protection for witnesses. The spokesperson also pointed to reforms passed this year to improve protection from secrecy offences for those providing intelligence and operational information to a royal commission.

Dan Jervis-Bardy

Labor conference to ‘showcase’ party: Albanese

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says Labor’s national conference will “showcase” what he describes as the “greatest political party” in Australia.

Albanese’s ministry met in Adelaide ahead of the start of the conference on Thursday, where MPs, trade unionists and rank-and-file members will gather to thrash out the party’s policy agenda for the next three years.

Gambling reform, fuel tax credits for miners, taxing gas exports, artificial intelligence and Israel and Palestine are among the most contentious issues up for debate, although Labor power brokers don’t expect any repeats of the major flare-ups of the past conference.

Speaking at the start of Wednesday’s ministry meeting, Albanese said:

We’re bringing the national conference here to Adelaide over the next three days. It’s an opportunity for our party members to have a direct say in the direction of the country and for us to engage. We represent the oldest and greatest political party in Australia. This is our 50th national conference. While other political parties have come and gone, we’ve continued to evolve, develop, we change with the times, and the party conference will reflect that over the coming few days in developing our platform that we’ll continue to take forward.

Ex-Socceroos captain receives ‘probable CTE’ diagnosis

Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade has revealed he has been diagnosed with probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), leading to renewed calls for all players under the age of 12 to be banned from heading the ball.


CTE is a progressive and neurodegenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts that can only be diagnosed after death, by autopsy.

There are criteria used in research that may indicate possible CTE but they are not advised for clinical use – the practice of diagnosing “probable CTE” is considered controversial.

The 64-year-old Wade received a diagnosis of probable CTE in late 2025 following the presentation of neurological symptoms and subsequent testing.

Wade, capped 84 times for Australia, has been told by his neurologist he will likely die because of it. He has spoken up about his experience, saying:

Football gave me so much. It gave me a life, a career, incredible experiences and the privilege of representing Australia.

But I also must be honest about the challenges I now face and the uncertainty that comes with living with a neurodegenerative condition.

I know my memory’s going. And I’ve been told by a number of people I’ve become a little bit short tempered, just snapped a bit.

- AAP

australia.title: This optical illusion is rarer than a rainbow and tricky to see in Australia. So what actually is a fogbow?
australia.snippet: Visible when the sun is behind you and the fog is ahead, conditions have to be ‘right in the Goldilocks spot’ to see a fogbow Get our bre...
australia.content:
When Marie Johnson woke up one foggy morning, she just had a feeling it would be eye-catching.

“It was first thing in the morning, when I was heading into town to work. I just thought I’ll quickly call in, get a photo of the fog with the old house,” says Johnson, who lives on a historic farm in Cobar, in outback New South Wales.

But then she turned around and saw the ethereal archway. “Oh my God, look at that. What is this? It’s like a rainbow, but it’s white,” she says.

The optical illusion, known as a fogbow, is rarer than a rainbow.

Ilana Cherny, a senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, says the conditions have to be just right to see one. “It really depends on you and the sun and the fog all being lined up in exactly the right way.”

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

world.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election
world.snippet: Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to t...
world.content:
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.

According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.

Since gaining independence from Portugal in 1975, the island country off Africa’s west coast has built a solid reputation for peaceful, competitive elections. But this year’s vote comes amid a tense political atmosphere and a lingering constitutional crisis.

The president, Carlos Vila Nova, is running for a second term as an independent, rather than as the candidate for the ruling Acção Democrática Independente (ADI), whom he represented when he was elected in 2021.

The tensions between Vila Nova and his former party began in January last year when he dismissed the prime minister, Patrice Trovoada. Trovoada’s replacement, the former justice minister Ilza Amado Vaz, resigned after just three days, before the current holder, Américo Ramos, took office.

On Sunday, Vila Nova will be running against four other candidates including the ADI parliamentary leader, Nito D’Abreu. Another former prime minister, Jorge Bom Jesus, attempted to withdraw his independent candidacy, but missed the deadline and remains on the ballot.

The main opposition party, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, is now part of a broad coalition backing the incumbent president, despite being staunch ADI opponents. Meanwhile, an ADI faction led by Ramos is backing D’Abreu. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the election will go on to a second round.

The businessman Domingos Monteiro, known as “Nino”, who has been president of the São Toméan Football Federation since 2015, was disqualified after the constitutional court ruled he did not meet the eligibility requirements. Monteiro was born on the island, but his parents never became naturalised citizens after moving from Cape Verde where they were born.

“The constitutional court is violating the principle of equal rights … It is time for descendants born in São Tomé and Príncipe to say no to discrimination, to the culture of xenophobia and persecution,” said Monteiro.

For voters, priorities include tackling government corruption, high inflation, severe youth unemployment, chronic fuel shortages, and frequent blackouts. Rivals of Vila Nova are hoping this will keep him from a second term and propel them to the presidency.

Corruption in São Tomé and Príncipe “is the greatest catastrophe the country has experienced in this half-century [of independence”, D’Abreu said at the presidential debate on Tuesday.

The country is seen as a trusted western ally for security and maritime trade in the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s biggest maritime piracy hotspots. It also has offshore oil deposits that make a significant contribution to its economy. Observer missions from the European Union, G7+ and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries are on the ground to monitor the polls.

world.title: ‘We are preserving a tradition’: how Ghana’s sensationalist film posters became collectible art
world.snippet: Hand-painted works are often wildly unfaithful to the movies they portray – reinterpretations that sometimes resulted in threats, insults...
world.content:
Sitting on his porch in Teshie near Accra, Heavy J dipped a brush into red oil paint and dabbed it carefully on to his canvas – a flour sack – adding blood to a knife being wielded by a man. Higher on the canvas, he had started on an outline of a skull.

Heavy J was creating a poster, but not as you might have expected for a horror film. Instead, it was for the animated fairytale The Little Mermaid. The man with the knife was not a killer but the film’s kind-hearted prince, Eric. The skull was also unrelated to the story. “We add more to make people interested,” said Heavy J, whose real name is Jeaurs Affutu.

Hand-painted film posters by local artists were a hallmark of Ghanaian film culture from the late 1970s to the early 2000s, used to advertise screenings for neighbourhood venues known as video clubs after organisers realised that the original posters were not attracting enough audiences.

Plot lines were regarded as little more than jump-off points for humorous and surreal flights of fancy. Artists working for different video clubs competed to make the best “forgery”, as they described their interpretations.

The practice began to wane around the turn of the century as more Ghanaians gained access to electricity and their own TV sets and video players. Many video clubs went out of business and painters pivoted to create other work. But by then the posters had attained global interest, popularised in books and foreign exhibitions, and old and rare paintings became prized collectibles.

There was a lull in interest in newly painted posters in the early part of the 21st century, but demand has risen, driven by online marketing and a receptive customer base of film lovers in the west.

Deadly Prey Gallery has been working with artists to preserve the culture of making hand-painted film posters, while helping meet the increased demand.

Named after an action film, the business was co-founded in 2012 by Brian Chankin, then a video rental store owner in Chicago, and Robert Kofi, a Ghanaian who, as a child, used to work as a “hype man” for video centres in his home town of Winneba and later started collecting and selling posters. They partnered after Kofi sold Chankin some works.

Deadly Prey Gallery works with 15 artists, including Heavy J, who has been painting posters for four decades, connecting them to online customers and shipping the artwork on completion.

Most orders come from the US. Old action, science fiction and horror films have the highest demand. Popular titles include The Exorcist and the Star Wars and Terminator franchises. And prices for commissioned pieces start at $600 (£450) and vary based on the canvas size and other customer preferences.

Kofi, who is based in Accra, is part manager and part editor. He identifies the artists most suited for each work, shares his vision of the posters with them and makes regular visits to their workspaces to review works in progress.

In a studio in Ashaiman, about 11 miles from Heavy J’s house, another artist called Stoger was working on two commissions: one for the horror film Poltergeist, and another for the experimental drama Gummo, which contains multiple acts of violence against cats and a scene in which a character eats spaghetti in a bath tub.

The poster showed three cats and a man in a bath with a plate of spaghetti in front of him. In his feedback that day, Kofi, speaking in Ga, a primary language of Ghana, told Stoger two of the cats were not aggressive enough and the food was too clean. “I want uglier cat scenes,” he later explained. “The spaghetti has to be dirtier.”

Stoger, born Benjamin Amartey, was a sculptor before developing an interest in films and becoming a poster painter in 1992. “I use my imagination to make scenes that will attract people so that they’ll love the poster,” he said.

The emphasis on exaggeration comes from an African tradition of “visualising the invisible”, said Joseph Oduro-Frimpong, the director of the Centre of African Popular Culture at Ashesi University and a poster collector himself.

“The posters’ audiences have not seen the film, so it’s impossible for them to know [whether they are accurate]. Therefore, the artists tap into what they call imaginative painting,” he said. “They will highlight these things and in doing so they incorporate things that are not in there. There is a kind of sensationalism to it.”

The reinterpretations at times resulted in threats, insults and even physical attacks from viewers who felt duped. Kofi laughed when he recalled an incident in the 1990s when people beat him up after they watched the action film Double Impact and realised it did not have a scene showing Jean-Claude Van Damme carrying out a beheading, as was illustrated on the poster.

At the Centre for National Culture in Accra, dozens of colourful posters from Deadly Prey Gallery are pinned on wooden walls. They include Jennifer Lopez launching an arrow at a snake in Anaconda, and a mouse coming out of Jamie Lee Curtis’ mouth in Halloween.

“We are preserving a tradition,” Kofi said of the poster-painting craft. “We are preserving a history.”

world.title: Seven Americans quarantining at Kenya Ebola facility after US travel ban, says aid group
world.snippet: Aid workers are first known people to quarantine at facility, which sparked huge opposition in Kenya Seven American aid workers who had b...
world.content:
Seven American aid workers who had been in Congo to fight the Ebola outbreak are quarantining at a new isolation facility in ⁠Kenya after the US government introduced travel ⁠restrictions, the head of a US charity ​employing them told Reuters.

The aid workers are the first known people to quarantine at the facility, which has sparked huge opposition in Kenya and is at the heart of a legal case in which a court has ordered the work to be ⁠suspended. Construction continued, however, according to US officials and satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters.

Washington’s new policy says American citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where there is an Ebola outbreak, must spend three weeks in a third country before entering the United States.

The US government is building ⁠the 50-bed bio-isolation unit on an air force base in central Kenya for asymptomatic Americans exposed to the virus in Democratic Republic of the Congo or Uganda. Many Kenyans are angered at what ​they see as the US offloading the health risk such patients pose.

Last month, Kenya’s ‌health minister announced an immediate halt to the facility’s ‌construction after he was found in contempt of court for failing to observe the order to halt work pending a final ruling.

“Samaritan’s Purse has seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team staff ‌members there,” Franklin Graham, president and CEO of Samaritan’s Purse, told Reuters in response to questions.

“None of them have any symptoms, but they are being quarantined by the Kenyan government for 21 days,” Graham said.

A US state department official told Reuters a group of asymptomatic Americans who had served on the frontlines of the Ebola response had “voluntarily moved to the Kenya facility for precautionary monitoring and isolation”.

“Kenyan authorities have authorized their movement into the facility under the observation of the US public health service clinicians,” the official said, adding that the decision was taken “strictly out of an abundance of caution”.

Kenyan health ministry officials did not immediately respond to calls or requests for comment ‌on the move. A senior Kenyan foreign ministry official said they had no information on it.

Another source familiar with the matter who asked for anonymity said that the group had arrived at the site in central Kenya on Monday and were sleeping in army cots in tents.

He said some ​had treated Ebola patients at the Christian aid group’s treatment centres in Congo but others had carried out work such as construction, with no direct contact with the sick.

“There is one potential high-risk exposure,” he said, adding that their health was being monitored. Kenyan authorities are not allowing the group to leave the facility to travel anywhere else in the country, he added.

The often fatal viral disease spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids from infected people or animals.

Samaritan’s Purse, which has been promised several million dollars from the Trump administration for the ⁠Ebola response, is an evangelical Christian group that works in disaster zones around the world.

It is one of the biggest foreign ​aid groups treating Ebola in Congo and has the largest number of ​Americans there, working closely alongside the World Health Organization to ​contain the outbreak. One of its US staff members who caught Ebola earlier this month was transferred to a hospital in Germany on Monday.
